scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

It’s a living, breathing conversation across generations. The Talmud itself is built on debates, contradictions, and reinterpretations (e.g., " *Torah is not in heaven*"—Bava Metzia 59b). Rabbis don’t just *apply* old rulings; they * wrestle* with texts, contexts, and human experience. **When you study Torah and rabbinic commentary, you’re not passively receiving instructions—you’re joining a 3,000-year-old dialogue.** - *Example*: A modern question about AI ethics might not have a direct Talmudic precedent, but the * principles* of *tzedek* ( justice), *shmirat ha’guf* ( bodily integrity), or * pikuach nefesh* ( saving a life) become tools for your own reasoning. **You’re not "copying" a rabbi—you’re using their framework to *think* for yourself.** - *Psychologically*: This is like a skilled musician using scales to compose original music. The tradition provides structure, but *your* creativity and judgment shape the outcome. If you’re truly *engaged* in the process ( studying, questioning, applying), the decision *does* feel like yours because you’ve actively participated in its formation. --- ### 2️️ ** "Feeling like your own" isn’t about being " original"— it’s about alignment** Many people equate " being your own" with " doing what feels instinctive or unique." But in Jewish thought, **your " self" is shaped by your values, relationships, and history—including tradition.** - *The Torah perspective*: The commandment to " *love your neighbor as yourself* " ( Lev Leviticus 19:18) isn’t about *your* instinctive feelings—it’s about * aligning* your actions with a higher ethical framework. When you internalize that, it becomes part of who you are. - *The psychological insight*: Studies show that when values are * internalized* ( not just externally imposed), decisions feel authentic. Think of a person who grows up in a family that values education—they don’t " feel like themselves" when they * reject* it, but when they * embrace* it as their own, it feels deeply personal. Tradition can be the same: if it’s part of your identity ( not just a external obligation), decisions aligned with it * feel* like yours. - *Caution*: If you’re following tradition * mechanically*—" I * have* to do X because the Talmud says Y"—without personal reflection, it * can* feel alienating. But if you’re * wrestling* with it (" *Why* does this matter? * How* does this apply to * my* life?"), it becomes a dialogue between your heart, mind, and tradition. **That’s where " your own" decisions emerge.** --- ### 3️️ ** The " instinct vs. tradition" tension is a Jewish * mitzvah*** Jewish tradition doesn’t see instinct and tradition as opposites. In fact, it * challenges* you to refine instinct through wisdom. - *The yetzer hara vs. yetzer hatov*: Jewish psychology teaches that " instinct" ( * yetzer hara*— the " evil inclination") isn’t inherently bad, but it needs * direction*.
